changes.before: Look for the accommodation cliff. Accommodations that exist for the current role are often lost during a rotation, a leadership cohort, or an interview process because nobody owns them across the transition. Name an owner for accommodations across every transition.
changes.after: Plan access across transitions. Before a rotation, leadership cohort, interview, or change of supervisor, confirm who will coordinate access arrangements with the person and the authorized accommodation process. Check what will continue and what needs review in the new setting.

changes.before: Accessible leadership programs by default: materials in advance, captioning, flexible participation formats, no timed or drag-based activities, and accommodations carried across every cohort event. The State of Minnesota Emerging Leaders Institute run by Minnesota Management and Budget is the verified public program; DHS-level pathways should be reviewed against the same standard.
changes.after: Design leadership programs for accessible participation: provide materials in advance, captioning, flexible formats, and alternatives to timed or drag-based activities. Review access arrangements across cohort events. Minnesota Management and Budget offers the Emerging Leaders Institute; use the current program information when considering this option.

changes.before: Make disagreement normal. Ask for the strongest case against your own idea before deciding. Thank the person who raised the concern, in front of others.
changes.after: Invite disagreement before deciding, including questions about your own proposal. Acknowledge the contribution in a way that respects the person's preferences and the sensitivity of the concern. Public recognition may be welcome, but should not expose a person who raised a private concern.

changes.before: In supervision. Ask what the person needs from you rather than telling them what you need. Make expectations explicit so people do not have to guess the unwritten rules.
changes.after: In supervision. Explain the work expectations and decisions within your responsibility, and ask what information, access, or support the person needs. Make expectations explicit so people do not have to infer unwritten rules.
